title: Latent Reward Registers for Diffusion Preference Alignment

paper.title: Latent Reward Registers for Diffusion Preference Alignment
paper.abstract:
Abstract Aligning diffusion models with human preferences usually relies on a sparse terminal reward evaluated on the final generated samples, presenting a severe temporal credit-assignment challenge across the multi-step denoising process. We propose Latent Reward Registers , a mechanism that estimates terminal preference directly from intermediate noisy latents by prepending learnable, position-free register tokens to the input sequence of a frozen Diffusion Transformer (DiT). This independent readout mechanism extracts latent reward evidence without altering the generator’s hidden states or velocity field.
The resulting dense, differentiable reward signal throughout the full denoising process facilitates two alignment strategies.
For training, Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (RG-OPD) distills reward-guided updates along on-policy trajectories, bypassing the computationally expensive rollouts of standard policy gradients.
For inference, Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) steers trajectories via magnitude-matched reward gradients without parameter updates.
Empirically, at high noise levels ( u = 0.8 u{=}0.8 ), the registers reach the highest pairwise accuracy among the evaluated latent reward models. Furthermore, RG-OPD outperforms online reinforcement learning baselines while reducing GPU hours by up to 33 × 33\times , and RGS establishes a new state-of-the-art among training-free methods, strictly enhancing both alignment and perceptual metrics. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/Guanys-dar/latent-reward-register

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: While diffusion and flow-matching models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-fidelity visual content, aligning these models with human preferences remains a critical challenge. Current methods generally rely on reward maximization ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . An external reward model evaluates the final generated image, and the generator is updated to maximize this scalar score, thereby improving perceptual quality and prompt alignment. Existing alignment methods typically fall into two paradigms. Reward backpropagation ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) unrolls the sampling trajectory to compute exact gradients from a differentiable reward model. While this enables fast optimization, it often leads to mode collapse. Alternatively, online reinforcement learning (RL) ( Black et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) formulates generation as a sequential policy optimized via policy gradients. This mitigates mode collapse but introduces high variance and low sample efficiency. Both paradigms face the same bottleneck: they rely on a single scalar reward evaluated only on the fully generated image. Because this terminal score cannot be easily attributed to specific intermediate steps, the supervision is severely delayed. To pass this delayed signal back, reward backpropagation must unroll long generation chains in memory, making it prone to over-optimization. Online RL, on the other hand, requires a large number of samples to keep gradient variance under control. Furthermore, adapting the generator to a novel reward function requires full retraining, as these terminal objectives offer no straightforward mechanism for test-time guidance. Our central insight is that DiT internal representations already encode sufficient evidence about the final output quality, well before the trajectory reaches a fully denoised state. Even under heavy noise, these features capture emerging global structure, prompt alignment, and overall trajectory viability. Rather than propagating a single endpoint score backward through a full rollout, we can therefore estimate the expected terminal preference directly from each intermediate latent, turning sparse terminal feedback into a dense, step-wise reward signal without requiring complex approximations. Building on this insight, we introduce Latent Reward Registers , a non-intrusive mechanism that turns a frozen DiT into an accurate, step-wise reward model. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , a small set of learnable, position-free register tokens is added as global readouts to aggregate reward-relevant evidence from the intermediate representations of the frozen transformer. A lightweight readout head then predicts the expected terminal preference directly from any intermediate latent. By differentiating this prediction with respect to the latent, we obtain a local reward gradient at every denoising step. Because the registers do not modify the generator’s hidden states or velocity predictions, the pretrained generative dynamics remain fully intact. As a result, the framework provides dense, differentiable reward supervision with minimal computation overhead. This dense reward signal supports alignment during both training and inference. For training, Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (RG-OPD) distills reward-guided updates along on-policy trajectories, bypassing the computationally expensive rollouts of standard policy gradients. For inference, Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) steers trajectories via magnitude-matched reward gradients without parameter updates, allowing multiple objectives to be composed at test time. Our contributions are summarized below. Figure 1: Latent Reward Registers vs. existing paradigms. Unlike conventional alignment methods that rely on delayed, sparse feedback from a clean image (Left) or require intrusive fine-tuning of the generator (Middle), our approach (Right) appends learnable registers to a frozen DiT. This enables the direct estimation of step-wise rewards from intermediate noisy latents ( z t z_{t} ). Consequently, we derive dense, differentiable reward gradients ( ∇ R \nabla R ) for generation while keeping the pretrained generative dynamics fully intact. • Reliable latent reward signals. Latent Reward Registers estimate step-wise rewards directly from intermediate noisy latents. Even at high noise levels, their pairwise ranking accuracy remains competitive with external reward models that require fully denoised images. • Efficient training-time alignment. By distilling register-guided on-policy trajectories, RG-OPD surpasses online RL baselines in alignment quality while reducing GPU hours by up to 33 × 33\times . • Effective inference-time alignment. RGS steers trajectories using the derived latent reward gradients without parameter updates, improving target rewards while maintaining a superior reward–quality trade-off relative to existing training-free sampling methods.

sections.heading: Diffusion Preference Alignment.
sections.text: Preference alignment for text-to-image generators is dominated by training-time methods. Reward backpropagation ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) differentiates through the denoising chain to optimize the generator directly, while online reinforcement learning ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) treats generation as a policy refined with policy gradients. These training-time approaches inherently bind the model to a fixed objective and incur heavy training costs. Furthermore, their reliance on sparse endpoint rewards complicates credit assignment across denoising steps. Training-free alignment offers an inference-time alternative, but existing schemes incur substantial computational overhead, whether through iterative search and optimization ( Yeh et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) or guidance gradients that become unstable at high noise levels ( Song et al., 2023 ) . Our approach instead extracts a dense, differentiable step-wise reward directly in the latent space, keeping alignment efficient at both training and inference time.

sections.heading: Latent Reward Models.
sections.text: Most reward models operate on clean, decoded images ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Kirstain et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Applying them to intermediate states would require forming a clean estimate from each intermediate latent via expensive VAE decoding at every step. Moreover, the resulting signals are noisy or unreliable on heavily corrupted inputs. Recent latent reward models instead evaluate noisy states directly, drawing evidence from selected internal features ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , early cross-attention maps ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , or separate process reward models ( Mi et al., 2025 ; Go et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Existing methods typically rely on heuristic feature engineering or computationally heavy auxiliary networks. Latent Reward Registers instead append lightweight, position-free register tokens to a frozen DiT, establishing a differentiable reward mechanism that avoids manual feature selection and leaves the base generator unaltered. This design directly supports both RG-OPD and RGS.

sections.heading: Test-time Guidance.
sections.text: Guidance methods steer a pretrained generator without retraining it. Classifier guidance injects the gradient of an auxiliary classifier into the score estimate ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , and classifier-free guidance (CFG) extrapolates between conditional and unconditional predictions to strengthen prompt adherence ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) ; the latter is standard in modern text-to-image diffusion. RGS continues this lineage: it leaves the generator and its native text guidance untouched and appends a reward-gradient correction whose magnitude is matched to the sampler’s own displacement. Because the correction is derived from latent registers at intermediate steps, sampling needs neither image decoding nor a separate reward-model backbone.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: To address the temporal credit-assignment problem in preference alignment, we construct a dense, differentiable reward signal directly from intermediate latent states, providing a unified supervision mechanism for both training and inference time alignment. The proposed framework consists of three core components: • Latent Reward Registers (Sec. 3.1 ): A lightweight mechanism that predicts the expected terminal preference using learnable register tokens and frozen DiT features. This auxiliary stream extracts step-wise reward signals from intermediate noisy latents without perturbing the original velocity field (Fig. 2 ). • Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (Sec. 3.2 ): A training-time alignment strategy that constructs detached one-step optimization targets along the student’s sampling trajectory. This bypasses backpropagation through complete denoising chains and eliminates the high variance of rollout-level policy gradients. • Reward-Guided Sampling (Sec. 3.3 ): An inference-time alignment technique that steers latent trajectories using magnitude-matched, step-wise reward gradients, requiring no additional parameter updates.

sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: Conventional image reward models supervise only the terminal generated image, and applying them to intermediate states would require repeated decoding that exposes the reward signal to noisy artifacts. DiT representations, in contrast, encode prompt alignment, layout, and appearance early in the generation process. We therefore introduce a lightweight side-stream readout that predicts terminal preference directly from a noisy latent z i z_{i} . Unlike a static feature probe, the register state persists across multiple frozen DiT blocks, accumulating evidence across depth. Because it derives representations from the backbone without altering the spatial token sequence, the side stream provides differentiable step-wise supervision while preserving the original velocity field.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate the framework along three axes: prediction accuracy of Latent Reward Registers on noisy latents, training efficiency of RG-OPD against RL and reward backpropagation baselines, and inference effectiveness of RGS relative to training-free sampling methods. Primary evaluations use SD3-Medium, with FLUX.1-dev providing cross-architecture evidence; we then ablate register designs and analyze noise robustness. Full protocols and extended analyses appear in the Appendix.

sections.heading: Setup.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We benchmark RG-OPD against reward-backpropagation (ReFL, AlignProp) and online RL methods (Flow-GRPO, Diffusion-NFT). All approaches update the generator weights. Evaluations utilize matched prompts, seeds, resolutions, and metric pipelines. HPSv3 and ImageReward serve as the optimization targets, while MUSIQ and CLIP-IQA assess reward-independent perceptual quality. Appendix B details the complete training protocol.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: RG-OPD attains the highest HPSv3 scores on both architectures while keeping a balanced multi-reward profile (Table 2 ). Reward-backpropagation baselines, by contrast, often maximize target metrics at the expense of visible perceptual degradation, a classic signature of reward over-optimization. In contrast, RG-OPD achieves a superior Pareto frontier between reward alignment and perceptual quality. Figure 4 shows this qualitatively: under matched prompts and seeds, RG-OPD preserves prompt-relevant content and perceptual quality without the artifacts exhibited by several baselines.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We compare RGS with the training-free baselines DNO and Demon under matched prompts, seeds, resolutions, and metrics. All methods keep the generator frozen; DNO and Demon optimize or search per sample using external reward models, whereas RGS uses analytical gradients from the latent reward register at each active step. HPSv3 and ImageReward quantify target alignment, and MUSIQ ( Ke et al., 2021 ) and CLIP-IQA ( Wang et al., 2023 ) measure no-reference perceptual quality. Extended protocol details are given in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Each single-head RGS variant improves its target metric relative to the CFG baseline while preserving perceptual quality, and RGS reaches the highest HPSv3 score among all evaluated training-free methods, with a favorable reward–quality trade-off under ImageReward optimization. Figure 5 gives the corresponding qualitative comparison; prompts and seeds are matched to hold input variation fixed, strictly isolating the observed improvements to the proposed guidance mechanism rather than prompt or seed selection. Beyond alignment accuracy, RGS demonstrates a distinct memory efficiency advantage. Because it shares the frozen denoiser backbone, peak memory stays comparable to unguided CFG and well below that of guided baselines, which require separate external scorer networks (Table 10 ). Figure 6: Training efficiency of RG-OPD. We compare the HPSv3 optimization trajectories of RG-OPD and Flow-GRPO against aggregate GPU hours on SD3-Medium and FLUX.1-dev. The curves indicate that RG-OPD requires fewer GPU hours to reach equivalent reward thresholds. This acceleration comes from the dense, step-wise gradients extracted from the latent reward registers. Figure 7: Effect of reward tilt ( r t r_{t} ) during RG-OPD training. Training dynamics are compared between r t = 0.20 r_{t}{=}0.20 and r t = 0.40 r_{t}{=}0.40 . The results show that a larger reward scale accelerates convergence and yields a higher peak performance. Moreover, the upward trend of the internal latent reward (a) remains consistent with the endpoint HPSv2 evaluation (b), indicating alignment between the intermediate proxy and the terminal objective. ImageReward (c) is evaluated as an independent, unoptimized metric to monitor the overall generation quality during the process.

sections.heading: Register design.
sections.text: The persistent register state is the main driver of accuracy. Removing the register causes the largest performance drop, while the skip-FFN design and the trainable query projection each add complementary gains (Table 4 ). Reducing the number of readout layers, by contrast, has little effect, indicating that persistent side-stream aggregation matters more than deep multi-scale feature extraction.

sections.heading: Training efficiency.
sections.text: Dense reward gradients provide continuous supervision throughout the denoising process, which accelerates convergence substantially relative to policy-gradient RL. On-policy trajectories meanwhile track the evolving student distribution. As Figure 6 shows, RG-OPD reaches Flow-GRPO-equivalent HPSv3 levels 14.0 × 14.0\times – 33.2 × 33.2\times faster in GPU hours on both backbones. To enable high-frequency monitoring of training dynamics, the efficiency trajectories are evaluated on a designated validation subset of 256 prompts. In contrast, the ultimate performance benchmarks in Table 2 are comprehensively assessed over the full 400/800 prompt–seed testing set, ensuring rigorous and unbiased final metrics.

sections.heading: Multi-head RGS.
sections.text: Multi-reward RGS balances competing objectives. Where single-head guidance targets one reward, the multi-head variant maintains a balanced profile across reward and perceptual metrics, consistent with the trends in Table 3 and Figure 8 . This supports the effectiveness of the equal-RMS aggregation strategy for multi-objective composition.

sections.heading: Robustness in high-noise regimes.
sections.text: DiNa-LRM performs competitively at low noise but degrades sharply as the latent inputs become uninformative, whereas the register retains accuracy throughout (Figure 3 ). This robustness matters precisely in the high-noise regime used for early guidance, where the register acts as a continuous step-wise signal rather than a late-stage endpoint proxy.

sections.heading: Additional analyses.
sections.text: Appendix E demonstrates that alignment improvements persist across varying sampling budgets, guidance strengths, and deterministic ODE solvers. It also analyzes the temporal accumulation of reward corrections along the generated trajectory. Appendix C empirically validates that the constituent register heads preserve the relative ranking distributions established by their corresponding endpoint reward models. Figure 8: Multi-head RGS. Multi-head reward gradients achieve a balanced performance across different reward metrics, compared to single-head RGS under identical settings.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we demonstrate that intermediate DiT representations capture terminal reward information early in the denoising process. Building on this insight, we propose Latent Reward Registers, a non-intrusive auxiliary stream that predicts endpoint rewards directly from intermediate noisy latents. The resulting dense reward field supports two alignment strategies. Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (RG-OPD) utilizes step-wise gradient supervision to outperform online RL baselines in efficiency and alignment, while avoiding the over-optimization typical of direct reward backpropagation. Furthermore, Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) applies magnitude-matched register gradients to steer generation without parameter updates, improving multi-objective target rewards while preserving perceptual quality. Ultimately, by resolving the credit assignment problem, this framework establishes a reliable latent reward model for diffusion RL.

sections.heading: Appendix F Future Work
sections.text: Our results show that reward-gradient guidance applied to noisy latents under a frozen generator improves preference alignment while keeping no-reference quality intact. Two directions seem especially promising for future exploration: (1) Few-Step Architectures and Video Generation. A natural next step is to evaluate latent reward registers on few-step distilled samplers and video diffusion models. For video generation, the register mechanism will require structural adaptations to enforce temporal consistency and coherent motion dynamics across high-dimensional latent sequences. (2) From RLHF to RLVR. The proposed framework is not inherently limited to subjective human preferences. We plan to explore its integration with RLVR, where the same non-intrusive latent readout could enforce objective criteria—ranging from high-level factual fidelity and spatial reasoning to low-level physical plausibility and strict structural constraints typically found in traditional inverse reconstruction problems.

Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Email: fengzipeng@kuaishou.com Peiqin Sun 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Kling Team Email: sunpeiqin@kuaishou.com Abstract Aligning diffusion models with human preferences usually relies on a sparse terminal reward evaluated on the final generated samples, presenting a severe temporal credit-assignment challenge across the multi-step denoising process. We propose Latent Reward Registers , a mechanism that estimates terminal preference directly from intermediate noisy latents by prepending learnable, position-free register tokens to the input sequence of a frozen Diffusion Transformer (DiT). This independent readout mechanism extracts latent reward evidence without altering the generator’s hidden states or velocity field. The resulting dense, differentiable reward signal throughout the full denoising process facilitates two alignment strategies. For training, Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (RG-OPD) distills reward-guided updates along on-policy trajectories, bypassing the computationally expensive rollouts of standard policy gradients. For inference, Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) steers trajectories via magnitude-matched reward gradients without parameter updates. Empirically, at high noise levels ( u = 0.8 u{=}0.8 ), the registers reach the highest pairwise accuracy among the evaluated latent reward models. Furthermore, RG-OPD outperforms online reinforcement learning baselines while reducing GPU hours by up to 33 × 33\times , and RGS establishes a new state-of-the-art among training-free methods, strictly enhancing both alignment and perceptual metrics. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/Guanys-dar/latent-reward-register 1 Introduction While diffusion and flow-matching models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-fidelity visual content, aligning these models with human preferences remains a critical challenge. Current methods generally rely on reward maximization ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . An external reward model evaluates the final generated image, and the generator is updated to maximize this scalar score, thereby improving perceptual quality and prompt alignment. Existing alignment methods typically fall into two paradigms. Reward backpropagation ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) unrolls the sampling trajectory to compute exact gradients from a differentiable reward model. While this enables fast optimization, it often leads to mode collapse. Alternatively, online reinforcement learning (RL) ( Black et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) formulates generation as a sequential policy optimized via policy gradients. This mitigates mode collapse but introduces high variance and low sample efficiency. Both paradigms face the same bottleneck: they rely on a single scalar reward evaluated only on the fully generated image. Because this terminal score cannot be easily attributed to specific intermediate steps, the supervision is severely delayed. To pass this delayed signal back, reward backpropagation must unroll long generation chains in memory, making it prone to over-optimization. Online RL, on the other hand, requires a large number of samples to keep gradient variance under control. Furthermore, adapting the generator to a novel reward function requires full retraining, as these terminal objectives offer no straightforward mechanism for test-time guidance. Our central insight is that DiT internal representations already encode sufficient evidence about the final output quality, well before the trajectory reaches a fully denoised state. Even under heavy noise, these features capture emerging global structure, prompt alignment, and overall trajectory viability. Rather than propagating a single endpoint score backward through a full rollout, we can therefore estimate the expected terminal preference directly from each intermediate latent, turning sparse terminal feedback into a dense, step-wise reward signal without requiring complex approximations. Building on this insight, we introduce Latent Reward Registers , a non-intrusive mechanism that turns a frozen DiT into an accurate, step-wise reward model. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , a small set of learnable, position-free register tokens is added as global readouts to aggregate reward-relevant evidence from the intermediate representations of the frozen transformer. A lightweight readout head then predicts the expected terminal preference directly from any intermediate latent. By differentiating this prediction with respect to the latent, we obtain a local reward gradient at every denoising step. Because the registers do not modify the generator’s hidden states or velocity predictions, the pretrained generative dynamics remain fully intact. As a result, the framework provides dense, differentiable reward supervision with minimal computation overhead. This dense reward signal supports alignment during both training and inference. For training, Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (RG-OPD) distills reward-guided updates along on-policy trajectories, bypassing the computationally expensive rollouts of standard policy gradients. For inference, Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) steers trajectories via magnitude-matched reward gradients without parameter updates, allowing multiple objectives to be composed at test time. Our contributions are summarized below. Figure 1: Latent Reward Registers vs. existing paradigms. Unlike conventional alignment methods that rely on delayed, sparse feedback from a clean image (Left) or require intrusive fine-tuning of the generator (Middle), our approach (Right) appends learnable registers to a frozen DiT. This enables the direct estimation of step-wise rewards from intermediate noisy latents ( z t z_{t} ). Consequently, we derive dense, differentiable reward gradients ( ∇ R \nabla R ) for generation while keeping the pretrained generative dynamics fully intact. • Reliable latent reward signals. Latent Reward Registers estimate step-wise rewards directly from intermediate noisy latents. Even at high noise levels, their pairwise ranking accuracy remains competitive with external reward models that require fully denoised images. • Efficient training-time alignment. By distilling register-guided on-policy trajectories, RG-OPD surpasses online RL baselines in alignment quality while reducing GPU hours by up to 33 × 33\times . • Effective inference-time alignment. RGS steers trajectories using the derived latent reward gradients without parameter updates, improving target rewards while maintaining a superior reward–quality trade-off relative to existing training-free sampling methods. 2 Related Work Diffusion Preference Alignment. Preference alignment for text-to-image generators is dominated by training-time methods. Reward backpropagation ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ) differentiates through the denoising chain to optimize the generator directly, while online reinforcement learning ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) treats generation as a policy refined with policy gradients. These training-time approaches inherently bind the model to a fixed objective and incur heavy training costs. Furthermore, their reliance on sparse endpoint rewards complicates credit assignment across denoising steps. Training-free alignment offers an inference-time alternative, but existing schemes incur substantial computational overhead, whether through iterative search and optimization ( Yeh et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) or guidance gradients that become unstable at high noise levels ( Song et al., 2023 ) . Our approach instead extracts a dense, differentiable step-wise reward directly in the latent space, keeping alignment efficient at both training and inference time. Latent Reward Models. Most reward models operate on clean, decoded images ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Kirstain et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Applying them to intermediate states would require forming a clean estimate from each intermediate latent via expensive VAE decoding at every step. Moreover, the resulting signals are noisy or unreliable on heavily corrupted inputs. Recent latent reward models instead evaluate noisy states directly, drawing evidence from selected internal features ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , early cross-attention maps ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , or separate process reward models ( Mi et al., 2025 ; Go et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Existing methods typically rely on heuristic feature engineering or computationally heavy auxiliary networks. Latent Reward Registers instead append lightweight, position-free register tokens to a frozen DiT, establishing a differentiable reward mechanism that avoids manual feature selection and leaves the base generator unaltered. This design directly supports both RG-OPD and RGS. Test-time Guidance. Guidance methods steer a pretrained generator without retraining it. Classifier guidance injects the gradient of an auxiliary classifier into the score estimate ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , and classifier-free guidance (CFG) extrapolates between conditional and unconditional predictions to strengthen prompt adherence ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) ; the latter is standard in modern text-to-image diffusion. RGS continues this lineage: it leaves the generator and its native text guidance untouched and appends a reward-gradient correction whose magnitude is matched to the sampler’s own displacement. Because the correction is derived from latent registers at intermediate steps, sampling needs neither image decoding nor a separate reward-model backbone. 3 Method To address the temporal credit-assignment problem in preference alignment, we construct a dense, differentiable reward signal directly from intermediate latent states, providing a unified supervision mechanism for both training and inference time alignment. The proposed framework consists of three core components: • Latent Reward Registers (Sec. 3.1 ): A lightweight mechanism that predicts the expected terminal preference using learnable register tokens and frozen DiT features. This auxiliary stream extracts step-wise reward signals from intermediate noisy latents without perturbing the original velocity field (Fig. 2 ). • Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (Sec. 3.2 ): A training-time alignment strategy that constructs detached one-step optimization targets along the student’s sampling trajectory. This bypasses backpropagation through complete denoising chains and eliminates the high variance of rollout-level policy gradients. • Reward-Guided Sampling (Sec. 3.3 ): An inference-time alignment technique that steers latent trajectories using magnitude-matched, step-wise reward gradients, requiring no additional parameter updates. 3.1 Reward Register Mechanism Motivation. Conventional image reward models supervise only the terminal generated image, and applying them to intermediate states would require repeated decoding that exposes the reward signal to noisy artifacts. DiT representations, in contrast, encode prompt alignment, layout, and appearance early in the generation process. We therefore introduce a lightweight side-stream readout that predicts terminal preference directly from a noisy latent z i z_{i} . Unlike a static feature probe, the register state persists across multiple frozen DiT blocks, accumulating evidence across depth. Because it derives representations from the backbone without altering the spatial token sequence, the side stream provides differentiable step-wise supervision while preserving the original velocity field. The persistent register state is the main driver of accuracy. Removing the register causes the largest performance drop, while the skip-FFN design and the trainable query projection each add complementary gains (Table 4 ). Reducing the number of readout layers, by contrast, has little effect, indicating that persistent side-stream aggregation matters more than deep multi-scale feature extraction. Training efficiency. Dense reward gradients provide continuous supervision throughout the denoising process, which accelerates convergence substantially relative to policy-gradient RL. On-policy trajectories meanwhile track the evolving student distribution. As Figure 6 shows, RG-OPD reaches Flow-GRPO-equivalent HPSv3 levels 14.0 × 14.0\times – 33.2 × 33.2\times faster in GPU hours on both backbones. To enable high-frequency monitoring of training dynamics, the efficiency trajectories are evaluated on a designated validation subset of 256 prompts. In contrast, the ultimate performance benchmarks in Table 2 are comprehensively assessed over the full 400/800 prompt–seed testing set, ensuring rigorous and unbiased final metrics. Multi-head RGS. Multi-reward RGS balances competing objectives. Where single-head guidance targets one reward, the multi-head variant maintains a balanced profile across reward and perceptual metrics, consistent with the trends in Table 3 and Figure 8 . This supports the effectiveness of the equal-RMS aggregation strategy for multi-objective composition. Robustness in high-noise regimes. DiNa-LRM performs competitively at low noise but degrades sharply as the latent inputs become uninformative, whereas the register retains accuracy throughout (Figure 3 ). This robustness matters precisely in the high-noise regime used for early guidance, where the register acts as a continuous step-wise signal rather than a late-stage endpoint proxy. Multi-head reward gradients achieve a balanced performance across different reward metrics, compared to single-head RGS under identical settings. 5 Conclusion In this work, we demonstrate that intermediate DiT representations capture terminal reward information early in the denoising process. Building on this insight, we propose Latent Reward Registers, a non-intrusive auxiliary stream that predicts endpoint rewards directly from intermediate noisy latents. The resulting dense reward field supports two alignment strategies. Reward-Gradient On-Policy Distillation (RG-OPD) utilizes step-wise gradient supervision to outperform online RL baselines in efficiency and alignment, while avoiding the over-optimization typical of direct reward backpropagation. Furthermore, Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) applies magnitude-matched register gradients to steer generation without parameter updates, improving multi-objective target rewards while preserving perceptual quality. Ultimately, by resolving the credit assignment problem, this framework establishes a reliable latent reward model for diffusion RL. References Black et al. (2023) K. Black, M. Janner, Y. Du, I.
